content.text: I'm checking task similarities (free) to design a test where rule-novelty and mapping-similarity point in opposite directions.
Noise is large, so I'm collecting more replicates on the key contrast (0-new-rule/low-similarity vs 3-new-rule/high-similarity).

input.command: python3 query.py submit '{"verdict": "part-based", "confidence": 0.88, "justification": "Trained L1-S1-M1 and L4-S4-M4. Tested recombinations with 0 new rules but low mapping similarity (L4-S1-M1 max sim 0.0; L4-S4-M1 and L1-S1-M4 max sim 0.375) against tasks with 3 new rules (L2-S3-M3 max sim 0.5625; L2-S2-M2 max sim 0.19). The 0-new-rule tasks were learned fastest (pooled mean about 19 examples, n=19; L4-S1-M1 mean 20 even though it shares no responses with either trained task). Both 3-new-rule tasks were slower (L2-S3-M3 mean 33, n=12; L2-S2-M2 mean 35, n=8). Their costs were the same even though their similarities differed a lot. One-new-rule L1-S1-M3 was in between (22, n=3). Cost tracks the number of new rules, not overall similarity, but tests are noisy."}'

content.text:
I submitted **part-based** with confidence 0.88. The deciding result is that a task built only from rules the learner already knew was learned faster than tasks with new rules, even though its responses matched no trained task. I used 42 of the 60 budget units.

**Design:** I trained the learner on two tasks, L1-S1-M1 and L4-S4-M4. I then used the free `compare` command to pick test tasks where the two hypotheses predict opposite orderings. "Similarity" below is the highest match with either trained task.

| Test task | New rules | Similarity | Mean examples to criterion |
|---|---|---|---|
| L4-S1-M1 | 0 | 0.0 | 20 (n=12) |
| L1-S1-M4, L4-S4-M1 | 0 | 0.375 | 18 (n=7) |
| L1-S1-M3 | 1 (M3) | 0.75 | 22 (n=3) |
| L2-S3-M3 | 3 | 0.5625 | 33 (n=12) |
| L2-S2-M2 | 3 | 0.19 | 35 (n=8) |

**Reasoning:**
- If the learner were holistic, L4-S1-M1 should have been the hardest task, since it gives a different answer from both trained tasks on every input. It was among the easiest.
- The two tasks with three new rules took about the same number of examples, even though one was much more similar to the trained tasks. Similarity made no visible difference.
- Cost rose with the number of new rules: about 19 for none, 22 for one, about 34 for three. That is the part-based pattern.

**Caveats:** The tests are very noisy. Single runs of the same task ranged from 1 to 47 examples. The main gap (about 19 vs 34) is roughly 2.5 to 3 standard errors, which is why I put confidence at 0.88 rather than higher. The one-new-rule result is based on only three runs.
